items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to enacting the "veterinary emergency response and mobility act of 2015"
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S250

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the education law, in relation to
enacting the "veterinary emergency response and mobility act of 2015"

 PURPOSE :

This bill provides for limited licensing exemptions for
specially-trained, out-of-state veterinarians, under specific
circumstances related to natural disaster response and high-volume
animal cruelty investigations.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1. Adds new subdivisions 14 and 15 to section 6705 of the
education law to provide limited licensure exemptions for
specially-skilled veterinarians during a declared disaster or
high-volume cruelty investigation when invited by the law enforcement
agency conducting such investigation.

Section 2. Adds new subdivisions 4 and 5 to section 6712 of the
education law to provide the same exemptions, under the same limited
circumstances, for specially-skilled veterinary technicians.

Section 3. Prescribes an immediate effective date.

 JUSTIFICATION :  From hurricanes and flooding to animal fighting and
other large-scale animal cruelty cases, law enforcement and emergency
management agencies rely heavily on specially-trained veterinarians to
rescue animals from life-threatening situations and mitigate
associated risks to human populations. This measure seeks to better
integrate these responders into the existing response framework by
recognizing the valid and current licenses of specially-trained
veterinary professionals invited into the State either by the
Department of Agriculture and Markets or by law enforcement to assist
with such incidents.

Expertise in the specialized fields of shelter medicine and forensic
veterinary medicine is critical to a successful response. Only a
veterinarian with shelter medicine experience can successfully oversee
an emergency or disaster response operation, which requires Incident
Command System (ICS) training and typically involves managing
long-term temporary housing for a large number of animals, preventing
infectious disease, following specialized sanitation protocols and
practicing behavior medicine. Responding to large-scale cruelty cases
also typically requires knowledge of ICS protocols, in addition to
long-term commitments and expertise in crime scene processing/forensic
veterinary medicine. Certain protocols must be followed by
veterinarians to collect and document evidence and follow chain of
custody rules as they process and care for animals.

Often, there is not a sufficient amount of New York-licensed
veterinarians available to provide the required expertise or meet the
volume of response needed in these situations. We saw this during New
York's response to Hurricane Irene and Super Storm Sandy, and most
recently in February, when the ASPCA worked with Attorney General
Schneiderman's Organized Crime Task Force to orchestrate the seizure
of over 4.000 roosters as a part of a three county cockfighting ring
raid.

Veterinary professionals typically hold a license to practice in only
their home state but emergencies or natural disasters and large-scale
cruelty cases can take place anywhere. While New York does have
mechanisms to recognize the valid and current out-of-state licenses of
volunteer health practitioners including veterinarians - in times of
emergency there is not express authority granted which would allow for
valid and current out-of-state licensed veterinarians to work in
animal response teams of sufficient number to effectively respond to
large-scale cruelty and emergency response cases. When veterinarians
are unable to deploy because of this licensing restriction, the
success of the operation is negatively impacted or in some cases, the
operation might not be able to happen at all.

Local veterinarians, of course, remain integral to the success of such
operations - indeed, long-term animal care is needed in many instances
following the conclusion of a given response or investigation but
having to rely too heavily on local veterinarians to fulfill all the
needs of a given animal response team can compromise the outcome of a
response to a large-scale cruelty case or emergency. Law enforcement
frequently requests that animal response teams keep operations
confidential prior to the execution of a warrant, which prevent
responders from securing the assistance of local veterinarians in
advance In addition, the vast majority of veterinary medicine
practitioners are small business owners who cannot leave their
practices on such short notice to assist. Of those who are able to
help, most can only offer one or two days at a time.  Because these
operations can last for many weeks, there is a need for ongoing
specialty care that almost always exceeds or exhausts the capacity of
a local veterinarian population, thereby resulting in a piecemeal
approach rather than thorough, methodical and consistent

care to a compromised population of animals.  This measure seeks to
responsibly ensure the provision of such specialty care when disaster
strikes or in support of state and municipal law enforcement cruelty
investigations, while ensuring that those services are provided only
for the duration of the investigation/response period.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY : 2014 S.7595/A.9786

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS : None

 EFFECTIVE DATE : Immediately
